en: Itivuttaka 47 Dukanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The one who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others, and the one who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, it was said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world... Now, friend Ānanda, what kind of person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? And what kind of person is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? “It is wonderful, friend, it is marvelous, friend! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One. For, friend, the Blessed One knows himself as one who is intent on his own welfare and on the welfare of others; he understands himself as one who is intent on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. Therefore, friend, listen and pay close attention; I will speak. “Yes, friend,” that monk replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Here, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust; he dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to ill will; he dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to restlessness and remorse; he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is the kind of person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. And here, friend, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust, having abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust; he dwells with a mind free from ill will, having abandoned the underlying tendency to ill will; he dwells with a mind free from sloth and torpor, having abandoned the underlying tendency to sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind free from restlessness and remorse, having abandoned the underlying tendency to restlessness and remorse; he dwells with a mind free from doubt, having abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is the kind of person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. These, friend, are the two kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Venerable Ānanda. Having said this, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Venerable Ānanda had departed, that monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and reported to the Blessed One everything that had occurred, exactly as it had happened. “Good, good, monk! Ānanda is wise, monk; Ānanda has great understanding, monk. If you were to ask me about this matter, I would have explained it to you in exactly the same way as Ānanda has explained it to you. This is indeed the meaning of what was said by me, and thus should it be understood. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Elated, that monk rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus was it said by the Blessed One, so I have heard. [End of] Itivuttaka 47. Dukanipāta, Second Chapter.
The Discourse on Vigilance.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:

"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell vigilant, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, joyful, and serene, and therein he should be one who gains insight at the proper time regarding wholesome states."
“Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu who dwells awake, mindful, clearly comprehending, concentrated, joyful, serene,
and who possesses timely insight into wholesome states, one of two fruits is to be expected:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"Listen to this while you are awake."
Those who are asleep, wake up!
For one who is asleep, waking is better;
for the wakeful, there is no fear.
He who is wakeful, mindful, clearly comprehending,
concentrated, joyful, and serene—
investigating the Dhamma rightly at the proper time, he...
Being one-pointed, he shall dispel the darkness.
Therefore, indeed, one should devote oneself to wakefulness:
a bhikkhu who is ardent, wise, and an attainer of jhāna.
“Having severed the fetter of birth and old age, one shall here and now touch unsurpassed enlightenment.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The tenth.
